We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. events.excerpt: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. events.excerpt: I would like to discuss a wallet design built around three components: Lindell 2-of-2 MPC signing, QR-only initialization, and encrypted NFC communication between a computer and a phone. The goal is to keep the convenience of a desktop wallet while ensuring that compromising either device alone does not provide unilateral signing authority. Lindell 2-of-2 MPC as the signing foundation The computer and phone each hold a private share of one joint signing key. Neither device holds the complete private key. Using a reviewed implementation of Lindell’s two-party ECDSA protocol , both devices interact to compute a signature without revealing their shares or reconstructing the complete private key. For Ethereum, the implementation would use secp256k1 and produce one ordinary ECDSA signature under the joint public key. The wallet can therefore use a normal Ethereum address without requiring an on-chain multisignature contract. The 2-of-2 requirement comes from the signing protocol itself: obtaining the computer’s share alone is insufficient, and obtaining the phone’s share alone is also insufficient. Both devices must participate in signing the same transaction. Initialize entirely through QR codes Initialization takes place before connecting the NFC reader. Each device generates its ow

events.excerpt: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion exam
events.headline: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home

events.excerpt: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. events.excerpt: Disclosure: I am the creator of Atomic Ownership Blockchains (AOB), which this repo covers in more detail than the other designs. What this is An open-source skill (SKILL.md format, Apache-2.0) that lets LLM agents analyze blockchain architectures on several independent dimensions instead of one number. The Nakamoto coefficient is a single-subsystem snapshot, goes stale, and is not comparable across consensus mechanisms, so the skill treats it as one input per subsystem, not a ranking. Dimensions currently covered: Node/validator concentration (NC per subsystem), stake/wealth concentration (Gini/HHI), client diversity, network/infrastructure Consensus dependency scope: does finalizing this transaction need agreement from parties unrelated to it? Privileged actors, payment finality authority, reliance on economic assumptions Sybil exposure, blast radius of one attack or one lost key, eclipse/network-view attacks, cost to participate It compares PoW, PoS, DAG, sharded designs and AOB, and reports each design’s validation level (production history, audits, testnet) separately from what its architecture does. In the Book of Revelation, this is associated with the “number of the beast,” leading some community members to view the milestone as noteworthy and somewhat amusing in the project’s history. Cardano organizes its operations into so-called epochs, which are five-day periods consisting of 432,000 one-second slots. events.excerpt: title: [Direct-to-AIP] Reserve Factor Updates Across Aave V3 and V2 Markets author: @TokenLogic created: 2026-11-12 Summary This publication proposes Reserve Factor updates on 54 reserves across 12 Aave V3 instances and the Aave V2 Ethereum market. At balances and rates as of 9 November 2026, the changes add about $3.5M of annualised revenue to the DAO and raise the blended RF from 12.0% to 12.7%. The proposal is part of the ongoing effort to streamline Aave V3. Motivation Overview Over the past months, the DAO has been streamlining Aave V3. Low-adoption reserves and instances have been wound down, Aave V2 has been frozen, and ongoing work aims to focus Ethereum Core on liquid, bluechip collateral, with assets that carry additional risk moving to Aave V4, where that risk can be priced. This proposal applies the same direction to the protocol’s revenue side. Every borrowable reserve exposes the DAO to collateral, oracle and liquidation risk. The RF compensates the DAO for carrying that risk. On many reserves today, the DAO keeps a small share of the interest on positions whose tail risk it fully underwrites. events.excerpt: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.”
events.headline: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC

events.excerpt: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. events.excerpt: The Statistical Reality of Coding Agents For technical decision-makers, leaderboard order can look more conclusive than the underlying comparisons allow. The ExpertCrowd-SWE study , an author-reported coding-agent benchmark submitted on November 9, 2026, provides a nuanced look at seven frontier coding agents. Rather than a simple ranking, the study identifies four statistical tiers, highlighting where evidence separates models and where it remains inconclusive. Four tiers, not seven distinct places The paper evaluated seven models on 100 expert-authored software-engineering tasks drawn from 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. Each model attempted each task five times. The paper reports 3,495 scored runs. Gemini 3.8 Flash had no valid run on one assigned task, so its score covers 99 tasks. The reported averages are: Opus 5.5 (67.3%), GPT-6 Astra (63.7%), Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0% across 99 tasks), Qwen 3.8 Max (33.5%), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (32.5%), and Grok 4.6 (32.2%). These averages form a four-tier pattern. The bottom three models—Qwen, DeepSeek, and Grok—are not statistically separated from one another in pairwise comparisons. Similarly, the top two models, Opus and Astra, are not statistically separated. While Opus leads Astra by 3.6 percentage points,
events.headline: ExpertCrowd-SWE finds four coding-agent tiers, but top pair remains unresolved

events.excerpt: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. events.excerpt: Russian exchanges may legally start crypto trading once the central bank approves their rules. Retail investors can buy only Bitcoin, Ethereum and USDT, with a yearly purchase cap. The Moscow Exchange is preparing a gradual pilot that starts in December. Crypto stays banned as a means of payment inside Russia, even as trading opens up. Russia’s stock exchanges will be legally allowed to run organized cryptocurrency trading from November 22 , 2026, after the Ministry of Justice registered a Bank of Russia ordinance setting out how trading in digital currencies and digital rights must work. The central bank confirmed the registration on November 11. November 22 is only the earliest legal opening date, since each exchange first needs the regulator to approve its trading rules, and the Moscow Exchange is aiming for December 1. For a central bank that wanted sweeping crypto restrictions less than five years ago, this puts Bitcoin on the same supervised venues where Russians already trade stocks and the ruble. Exchanges need their rulebooks approved first The ordinance builds on the conditions for organised trading in digital currencies that the Bank of Russia first drafted in July.
